extracted.intended_audience: EU trademark attorneys, EUTM examiners, IP practitioners and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal criteria used by the EU Boards of Appeal/Grand Board to assess registrability, invalidity, revocation and oppositions of EU trade marks, including distinctiveness, descriptiveness, likelihood of confusion, acquired distinctiveness, territorial perception and procedural admissibility. Focused on interpreting CTMR/EUTMR provisions in appeal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive character / minimum degree of distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment whether the sign 'lacks the minimum degree of distinctiveness' for the goods and services concerned and 'is not capable of being perceived as an indication of commercial origin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the sign as a whole; determine whether the relevant public can perceive it as denoting trade origin rather than merely describing kind, contents, purpose or promotional claims. Visual elements (colours, font, background) must be capable of diverting attention from any non-distinctive message to salvage distinctiveness; if they do not, refusal under Article 7(1)(b) follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptiveness (Article 7(1)(c)/7(1)(b) EUTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sign may 'merely describe the kind, contents and purpose of the goods and services' and be rejected as descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify clear and direct link between word/element and the goods/services (examples: 'easyBank' – 'easy' + 'bank' directly denotes banking services). Juxtaposition of commonplace terms that do not create unusual impression remains descriptive even with typeface/background. Apply Common Communication on Distinctiveness for figurative marks containing descriptive/non-distinctive words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant public (definition and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the relevant public by territory, language and level of attention: e.g., 'English-speaking specialists', 'specialists outside the medical sector', 'all consumers in the EU', or German-speaking population for geographic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor perception analysis to the linguistic and experiential characteristics of the relevant public (professionals vs public at large), and account for degree of attention (average, low, specialised/informed user).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired distinctiveness by use (Article 7(3) EUTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A later showing of distinctiveness through use may allow registration where a sign was otherwise non-distinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must demonstrate that consumers, in a trade context, associate the sign with a particular undertaking. Mere general fame or association with a historic or political event (e.g., 'Brexit') or seasonal/insignificant use (e.g., 'Easter bunnies') is insufficient. Assess whether use covers a sufficiently significant part of the market and trade exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy / Principles of morality (Article 7(1)(f) EUTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign may be refused if contrary to accepted principles of morality or public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the sign expresses an opinion, incitement to crime, emblem for terrorism, sexism or racism, or carries negative moral connotations. Mere upset among part of the public about a democratic decision does not by itself render a sign immoral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical representation vs actual use
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing registrability the version in which the sign is actually used should not be taken into account in place of the sign as graphically represented on the Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate distinctiveness based on the register representation; if re-opening of case produces new evidence about actual use, Grand Board may decide on grounds based on that new evidence but should respect the registered graphical representation for core assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colours/font/background cannot overcome nondistinctive message
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours, typeface and background are relevant but 'are unable to divert the attention of the public away from the non-distinctive message conveyed by the word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the overall get-up produces distinct commercial origin perception beyond the literal/descriptive meaning. If decorative elements reinforce the non-distinctive concept (e.g., Union Jack background accentuating 'Brexit'), they will not save the mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of confusion – factors for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing Article 8(1)(b) (relative grounds), compare signs and goods/services taking into account visual, aural, conceptual similarity, nature and purpose of goods, method of use, clientele, distribution channels, legislative regulations and commercial interchangeability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider degree of similarity in each dimension, whether non-distinctive elements are dominant, and the overall impression on the relevant public. A risk of association cannot be based on a non-distinctive element alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of goods – similarity/dissimilarity criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare goods/services to determine similarity or dissimilarity (e.g., 'vodka' vs 'mineral water' are dissimilar because of differing nature, alcohol presence, manufacturing process and supermarket placement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factors such as nature, composition (presence/absence of alcohol), manufacturing methods, regulatory regime, distribution channels, consumer purpose and whether goods are interchangeable or in competition. Do not rely on speculative arguments (e.g., possibility of mixing drinks) to find similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of attention of the relevant consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment must account for the degree of attention of the relevant consumers (ranging from average to low or specialised/informed users).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower degree of attention increases likelihood of confusion; when relevant public includes specialists, apply a higher threshold and consider specialist perception. The 'informed user' in design matters is particularly observant due to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant element in complex marks
rubrics_metrics.description: In a complex sign, establish whether any element is dominant for the overall impression; weak or descriptive elements cannot be the dominant element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all elements are descriptive/non-distinctive they share equal value; a proprietor cannot claim dominance for a weak element to establish confusion. Evaluate figurative/word elements for dominance and distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of a trade mark
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark must function as an indication of commercial origin; promotional promises or laudatory statements ('la qualité est la meilleure des recettes') are not capable of indicating origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the sign will be perceived by consumers as a simple marketing incitement or as an indication of origin. Plain promotional language in ordinary terms is normally non-distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shapes giving substantial value to the goods (Article 7(1)(e)(iii) EUTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shapes which give substantial value to the goods (e.g., traditional Easter bunny shape) are excluded from registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the shape determines consumer behaviour and purchase decisions because of tradition/appearance. If shape confers substantial value to the product, refusal under Article 7(1)(e)(iii) is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-filing and admissibility / confirmatory acts and legal certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant re-filing the same trade mark for the same goods/services bears the onus of showing why a re-examination is justified by new factors; appeals against confirmatory acts are not admissible to reopen definitive decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect res judicata and legal certainty: avoid allowing re-filing to circumvent final Board/Court decisions. If the Office's reply to a second application repeats earlier arguments, that alone does not show a fresh examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers may only be entered at the application stage; requests to record a disclaimer after registration are inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 37(2) CTMR wording circumscribes disclaimers to pre-registration. Any post-registration disclaimer recordal should be refused as inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications and perception (Article 7(1)(c) CTMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographic term constitutes a 'characteristic' of goods/services when the relevant public perceives it as indicating geographic origin; unknown geographical indications do not constitute descriptiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether, on the filing date, the relevant public (by language/territory) perceived the term as a place name and as origin for the goods/services concerned; major or economically important regions are likely to be known and perceived as geographic origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorisation for non-use revocation / genuine use
rubrics_metrics.description: Within broad category specifications (e.g., 'footwear' in Class 25), the Board may identify subcategories (e.g., 'women's footwear') and assess genuine use accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse market realities, consumer purchasing purpose, evidence provided (sales, product examples) and established case-law criteria to determine whether a subcategory is sufficiently homogeneous and not too narrow for proof of genuine use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to prove saturation of prior art for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove saturation of the prior art/state of the market, parties must present clear, precise and coherent evidence (market surveys, trade fair reviews, statements from trade associations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saturation is a high evidentiary threshold: absence of sufficiently specific evidence undermines claims based on saturation when assessing individual character or novelty of designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed user standard for designs / overall impression
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'informed user' is a particularly observant user, whose greater attention and knowledge affects perception of overall impression and differences between designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing designs, determine whether differences (planes, diagonals, rim, depth) would escape an informed user's notice; small but notable differences may change overall impression for an informed user.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial use / proof of genuine use for subcategories
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine use may be established only for a subcategory of goods covered by an earlier mark (principle of partial use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish which subcategory has been genuinely used (e.g., 'rum' within 'alcoholic drinks') via concrete evidence; then compare degree of similarity across contested goods (identical, highly similar, low similarity) using specific factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of market and filing practice as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may take into account market realities and EUTM application filing practice (applicants distinguishing types by wording) when assessing subcategories and perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market segmentation and common filing practices as contextual evidence that certain subdivisions (e.g., by gender or product type) are traditionally accepted and meaningful in consumer perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence, acquiescence and strength of mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic coexistence of identical signs used by organisations with shared origin can prevent third parties from arguing the sign is weak; evidence of peaceful coexistence and acquiescence matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider goodwill established by long-standing users and whether competitors' ability to use descriptive components is an accepted consequence; weigh evidence of reputation and prior use in relevant territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of complex marks (3D + word/device) for classification as 3D marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a mark combines a three-dimensional shape with a prominent word/device element, determine whether it qualifies as a three-dimensional trade mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider case-law (e.g., C‑445/13 P, Bottle) and whether the word/device element is placed on the most visible part; remittal to Boards may be necessary where later case-law affects classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of well-known facts and evidence of reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-known facts (e.g., widely known geographic regions, publicised events) and evidence of reputation (sales figures, press articles) are relevant in assessing perception, reputation and likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require substantiation: claims relying on reputation or well-known facts must be supported by concrete evidence showing the extent and territorial scope of recognition on the filing date.
